newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Finally some numbers to crunch. [CORRECTED 11:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Finally some numbers to crunch. [CORRECTED 11:30 GMT]

text.p: Data-starved for almost a week now, U.S. credit market players will have something to chew on Friday when fresh reports on the economy's manufacturing and real estate sectors will be released, analysts said.
Market pundits added, however, that the new data might be a bitter pill to swallow.
The day starts with the durable goods report for September at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, which is expected to show a solid rebound from the low levels registered in the previous month.

In a Reuters poll, economists predicted a 2.0 percent rise in overall durable goods orders in September, against a 3.2 percent drop in the previous month. The ex-defense numbers are seen up 1.3 percent against a 3.6 percent fall in August.
Anxiety ahead of the data gained momentum after rumors late in the week said that a possible surge in aircraft orders could lift durable goods orders even further, analysts said.

"The market's been nervous about durables all week," said Michelle Colley Laughlin, Treasury strategist at Prudential Securities Inc. "I think the market is bracing for bad news, and if indeed we get bad news the market will be hurt."
For some, however, caution is the word.

"Durables will probably show a nice increase...But you've got a saw-tooth pattern in that series most of the year and the increase will really just reverse last month's decline," said John Williams, managing director at BT Securities Corp.
"That would leave the overall series still in a relatively sluggish mood...The manufacturing sector is continuing to lag the rest of the economy. It's doing okay, but it's not strong," Williams said.
At 1000 EDT/1400 GMT (corrects GMT time), market participants will take in existing home sales for September.
In a Reuters survey, economists see home sales staying mostly flat at 4.11 million in September, against 4.13 million in the previous month.
"In general the housing market is moving sideways. It's sideways to slightly lower," Laughlin said.
The University of Michigan's final consumer confidence index for October will also be issued on Friday. The indicator is expected around 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. (corrects GMT time)
If all numbers come in as expected, analysts said the outlook for what the Federal Reserve might do next is likely to remain mostly unchanged.

"I don't think tomorrow's data will shed a light on what the Fed might do next," Williams said, adding he expects the central bank to stay on hold for a while with the next move being a tightening and taking place not until early next year.

Although analysts did not discount some price volatility after the numbers on Friday, they said the Treasury market is expected to remain trapped in a trading range between 6.7 and 7.0 percent on the 30-year bond yields.
"Tomorrow we're likely to stay there. Next week we have the potential to move outside of that range, depending on the data," Laughlin said.
Analysts said the market was also still grappling with the supply of two- and five-year notes from earlier in the week.

"We have these two auctions still kicking around... (But) I think a big number (on durables) could give people pause on buying at the top-end of the range," said Lee Youngdahl, economist at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co Inc.

On Thursday, the Fed added reserves to the banking system via overnight and 14-day fixed system repurchase agreements. The Fed cancelled the operations once due to a technical glitch and then repeated them shortly after.
Fed funds are seen opening at 5.13 percent Friday, below the Fed's 5-1/4 percent target. The T-bond was down 10/32 in late trade on Thursday at 98-21/32 to yield 6.86 percent.
